articles.title: Global Wheat Study Revises Heat and Drought Losses - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: Global Wheat Study Revises Heat and Drought Losses  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
An upgraded global wheat model estimates average yield penalties of 9.7% from drought, 5.8% from heatwaves and 13.3% when both coincide. These are modeled historical effects—not a measured drop in harvests or a forecast.
The results, published in Nature Food on 8 October 2026, cover 1981–2015. Their importance is partly methodological: a refined crop model reproduced past weather-linked yield losses more accurately than a multimodel benchmark. The study does not say that global wheat production fell by those percentages in any particular year.
What changed in the model?
Yuchuan Luo of Southwest University’s School of Geographical Sciences in Chongqing and colleagues modeled global wheat yields on a roughly 10-kilometre grid, combining crop growth, weather and agricultural data. The model’s skill improved 30% for drought, 20% for heatwaves and 7% for compound events versus a multimodel ensemble. Those are simulation-skill gains, not extra percentage points of yield loss.
The supplement also makes the calibration choice visible: the primary configuration used fully irrigated conditions, while an alternative used each grid cell’s actual irrigated or rain-fed system. The alternative improved correlation with observed national yields (R² = 0.70), but its centered RMS deviation (2.24 tonnes per hectare) and relative yield error (45.7%) were higher than in the primary calibration. It also consistently underestimated observed event losses.
The model does not simply count tonnes harvested. It compares yield anomalies in extreme-event years with anomalies in years without those disasters, then tests performance against historical crop statistics. A better representation of crop response can change estimated impact size even when the weather record is unchanged.
Supporting material describes subnational validation data for 54 countries and tests against documented disasters. That is broad evidence, but each 10-kilometre grid cell is not a field measurement. It smooths local differences in varieties, soils, planting dates, management and water access; results are regional-scale model estimates.
How should readers read the percentages?
The headline averages—9.7% for drought, 5.8% for heatwaves and 13.3% for compound drought-and-heat events—describe modeled average yield losses over the historical study period. They are not observed changes in national harvest totals, year-on-year global output declines, or predictions for the next crop season. The compound-event estimate should not be added to the drought and heat estimates: the categories represent overlapping stresses, not three independent losses.
- “Yield loss” is not the same measure as tonnes lost from a national harvest.
- A historical average describes the study period, not the next season’s expected result.
- Drought, heatwave and compound-event estimates overlap; adding them would misstate the result.
The supplement provides a regional scale example. For Australia, it reports average model-estimated wheat-yield losses of 21% during drought events and 32.2% during compound drought-and-heat events over 1981–2015. Those figures describe modeled yield response in the study’s event analysis; they are not a tally of Australian wheat tonnes lost, a statement about every farm, or a current forecast. They also should not be transferred to other countries as if growing conditions were interchangeable.
The authors also report that irrigation buffered some modeled damage, while that counteracting effect weakened as extreme events intensified. This is not a blanket recommendation to irrigate. The model result does not establish that water is available, affordable or sustainable at a particular location, nor that irrigation can remove losses under all combinations of heat and drought.
What does the trade study add?
A separate peer-reviewed 2026 study in Environmental Research Letters examines another part of the risk chain: how concurrent heatwaves and drought can affect wheat production and cross-border trade. It combines national agricultural statistics, bilateral trade information and historical climate data. Its abstract reports reduced production and exports in major wheat-producing countries, particularly those where wheat is predominantly rain-fed, while effects on importers’ domestic supply vary.
That trade analysis is distinct from the Nature Food crop-model paper. It does not supply the 9.7%, 5.8% or 13.3% averages, and those yield estimates do not by themselves predict export volumes or import prices. The published abstract reports that effects on importers’ domestic supply varied, but it does not provide a country ranking or comparable national loss figures.
Where the findings stop
These papers help researchers and readers understand how historical climate extremes can affect wheat yields and why model structure matters. They do not provide a 2026/27 production forecast, a food-price outlook, or a purchasing or planting instruction. A global historical average is not a direct measure of the conditions facing a particular farm, country or shipment.
The supporting validation table covers 54 countries but has no Kenya-specific wheat estimate. Wheat seasons, cultivars, soils, irrigation access and management differ across regions, so neither the global averages nor Australia’s modeled result can be converted into Kenyan farm advice. They also cannot establish Kenyan import exposure or local flour prices; those questions require current country-specific yield, trade, stock and market evidence. The safe conclusion is narrower: improved modeling revises estimates of past wheat-yield damage, while local decisions need locally validated data.
How did this story land?
No sign-in required. Choose up to two. This captures your response to the story—it is not a vote on whether the reporting is true.

articles.title: Everyone Wants a Piece of US LNG - East Daley
articles.summary: Everyone Wants a Piece of US LNG  East Daley
articles.full_text:
Already in high demand, US LNG has become an even hotter commodity thanks to the Iran conflict. Market desperation has reached a point that QatarEnergy, the world’s largest LNG supplier, is reportedly in talks for term contracts with US projects.
Qatar’s interest in US LNG is only the tip of the iceberg. With the Strait of Hormuz closure stretching into a seventh month, global LNG supply has tightened to extreme levels, triggering energy shortages and higher prices in Asia and Europe.
QatarEnergy previously met about 20% of global LNG demand, but has seen its output severely curtailed since March. The company declared a force majeure after Iran struck its Ras Laffan liquefaction complex at the outset of the war, causing extensive damage to two of its 14 liquefaction trains. The trains, representing ~12.8 Mtpa of capacity, are expected to require three to five years to repair. Restrictions on Strait of Hormuz shipping have further limited Qatar’s ability to move cargoes from the other trains. QatarEnergy has repeatedly extended its force majeure, currently in place through November. Roughly 80% of Qatar’s LNG shipments typically go to Asian buyers.
QatarEnergy has worked to meet its term contracts by purchasing LNG from US facilities. Over the summer, the company bought 33 spot cargoes from Venture Global (VG). VG’s Plaquemines facility remains in its commissioning phase but has been running at or above nameplate capacity since November 2025. The company expects Phase 1 of the facility to enter commercial operations in late 2026.
Beyond the spot purchases, Reuters reports that QatarEnergy is seeking contracts for 2–3 Mtpa through 2031, shifting away from more expensive spot cargoes and toward longer-term supply agreements. The company is reportedly in talks with Cheniere Energy (LNG), Venture Global and Woodside Energy (WDS).
Venture Global currently has 39 Mtpa of production capacity and only 30 Mtpa committed under sales and purchase agreements (SPAs), leaving roughly 9 Mtpa available for spot cargoes or additional long-term contracts. When its CP2 expansion comes online later this decade, VG’s production capacity will increase to 65 Mtpa. With 48 Mtpa contracted, the company would have nearly 20 Mtpa available.
Cheniere has 64 Mtpa of available production capacity, including the recently finished Corpus Christi Stage 3 project. With roughly 45 Mtpa committed under SPAs, the company will have significant capacity available to serve the market.
QatarEnergy is far from the only buyer looking to US LNG projects. Companies in Thailand, Pakistan and Bangladesh are reportedly discussing long-term agreements with US suppliers as they seek to secure LNG amid the uncertainty in the Middle East. China Gas also recently signed a 20-year agreement with VG for 0.5 Mtpa from the company’s portfolio. INPEX CEO Takayuki Ueda recently said it is weighing an investment in a US LNG project to further diversify its portfolio.
The US is already the largest LNG supplier to the world, and its lead is poised to grow over the next 5-10 years. East Daley Analytics projects total US LNG production capacity could exceed 50 Bcf/d (390 Mtpa) by 2035, giving the industry even more room to expand its role as a reliable global gas supplier. – Emily Cecchini Tickers: LNG, VG, WDS.
Can Crude and NGL Markets Keep Pace with the US LNG Boom?
Rising US LNG feedgas demand has the potential to float all boats — but only if crude oil and NGL markets can support the growth.
Reaching nearly 26 Bcf/d of LNG feedgas demand by the end of 2027 will require producers to drill aggressively across the Permian, Haynesville and Northeast. In the Permian especially, that growth depends on steadier crude prices, to give producers the confidence to commit capital, subscribe to new pipeline capacity and fill the infrastructure midstream companies must build.
Join East Daley Analytics on Wednesday, Sept. 30 as we examine the cross-commodity conditions required to keep the LNG growth story on track:
- What crude price environment will support sustained drilling and pipeline investment?
- Could Permian crude constraints limit associated gas production?
- Where could NGL processing, takeaway and export bottlenecks emerge?
- Which companies are best positioned to capitalize?
LNG demand may be the rising tide — but crude and NGL markets will determine whether all boats can rise with it.
Join East Daley Analytics on Sept. 30 at 10:00 am MT for a discussion at the intersection of energy. Click here to reserve your spot today.

The Canada S&D completes our North American model, providing a fully integrated supply and demand forecast for crude oil and natural gas. articles.title: Natural Gas Price Forecast — NG Futures ($3.19) Slip on Mild Weather Despite 67 Bcf Storage Miss — $3.30 Test Into Expiry - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: Natural Gas Price Forecast — NG Futures ($3.19) Slip on Mild Weather Despite 67 Bcf Storage Miss — $3.30 Test Into Expiry  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Henry Hub ($3.19) Caught Between a Shrinking Storage Surplus and Mild Late-October Weather — $3.10 to $3.35 Range
The storage surplus fell from 148 Bcf to 45 Bcf above the five-year average in five weeks | That's TradingNEWS
Key Points
- November natural gas futures fell about 1.4% to $3.19 after hitting a nearly three-week high of $3.283 on October 13.
- The EIA’s 67 Bcf injection missed the 76 Bcf forecast, cutting the storage surplus to 45 Bcf above the five-year average.
- Lower 48 production averages 110.8 Bcf/d in October, down from record highs of 113.3 Bcf/d in August and September.
Natural gas futures for November delivery are trading at $3.19 per million British thermal units, down about $0.05, or 1.40% to 1.50%, on the day. Futures slumped at the start of Friday’s session after Thursday’s gain. Traders are weighing a lean storage report, low production, an Appalachian pipeline outage and strong LNG demand against forecasts for mild weather through the end of the month.
Thursday was a good day for the bulls. November futures rose about 2% after the Energy Information Administration reported a smaller-than-expected storage injection, daily production dropped to a five-month low and weather forecasts showed higher demand over the next two weeks than earlier expected. Prices traded near $3.25 ahead of the report.
The week’s high came on Monday. On October 13, November futures reached $3.283, a nearly three-week high. Since then, prices have pulled back about 2.8%.
Natural gas is up sharply over the past month. The November contract has gained 9.9% to 10.0% over 30 days. Over 12 months, prices are up about 6%. A year ago, Henry Hub spot averaged $3.19 in October 2025, nearly the same level as today.
The November contract expires on October 28. After that, the December contract becomes the front month. December futures trade at a premium to November, reflecting expected winter heating demand.
Henry Hub spot prices have been volatile. The physical price at Henry Hub, Louisiana, was $3.22 on October 14, up from $3.14 on October 13 and $3.10 on October 12 and October 9. On October 8, spot traded at $3.24. Henry Hub cash has held a premium to NYMEX futures this week.
The monthly averages show a steady recovery from summer lows. Henry Hub spot averaged $2.79 in August, $2.89 in July and $2.95 in September. October is running higher.
The 2026 picture has been dramatic. Henry Hub spot averaged $7.72 in January during Winter Storm Fern, which drove record storage withdrawals. It fell to $3.62 in February and hit summer lows near $2.79. The EIA has cut its 2026 annual price forecast by more than 20%, from $4.31 in February to $3.44 in August.
The setup is a tug of war. Supply is tight in the short term: production has fallen sharply from record highs, the storage surplus is shrinking and LNG exports remain strong. But demand is soft, with mild weather expected through October 29 and storage still 45 Bcf above the five-year average. The next sections map both sides.
Storage: 67 Bcf Build Misses the 76 Bcf Forecast
Thursday’s storage report was the most bullish data point of the week.
The EIA reported a net injection of 67 billion cubic feet for the week ending October 9. The consensus forecast was 76 Bcf. Some estimates were as high as 74 to 75 Bcf. The prior week’s injection was 85 Bcf.
The 67 Bcf build was well below historical norms. The five-year average injection for the same week is 90 Bcf. Last year’s injection for the same week was 80 Bcf. This year’s build was 23 Bcf below the five-year average and 13 Bcf below last year.
Total working gas in storage rose to 3,567 Bcf. That is 45 Bcf, or 1.3%, above the five-year average of 3,522 Bcf. It is 143 Bcf, or 3.9%, below last year’s level of 3,710 Bcf. Total storage remains within the five-year historical range.
The surplus is shrinking fast. On September 4, storage was 148 Bcf above the five-year average. Five weeks later, the surplus has fallen to 45 Bcf. That is a drop of 103 Bcf in the cushion that had been weighing on prices.
All regions posted increases except the Pacific. The Midwest led all regions. The East rose 22 Bcf to 884 Bcf, 3.3% above its five-year average.
The South Central region is the weak spot. All regions are above the five-year average except South Central and South Central salt. Salt storage in South Central, which can be filled and drawn quickly, stands at 236 Bcf. That is 21.9% below last year and 15.4% below the five-year average. Salt caverns are the market’s fast-response storage. Low salt levels mean less buffer for sudden cold snaps.
The injection season is nearly over. The EIA forecasts that inventories will build by 328 Bcf during October to reach 3,850 Bcf by the end of the month. That would leave storage 2% above the five-year average entering the heating season on November 1. Mild weather could extend injections into mid-November.
The next storage report is October 22. Early estimates for the week ending October 16 will set the tone for next week.
For the forecast, the storage trend is bullish. A shrinking surplus means less cushion for winter. Another injection below 70 Bcf next week would push the surplus toward zero and support prices above $3.30.
Production: Eight-Month Low After Hurricane Isaias and Pipeline Outages
Lower production is the main reason the storage surplus has shrunk.
U.S. Lower 48 gas output averaged 110.8 billion cubic feet per day so far in October, according to financial data firm LSEG. That is down from record highs of 113.3 Bcf/d in August and September. The drop of 2.5 Bcf/d is significant in a market where small changes in supply move prices.
Daily output fell further this week. On October 13, production was on track to drop to an eight-month low of about 107.1 Bcf/d. On Thursday, output dropped to a five-month low on a daily basis.
Several factors drove the decline. Hurricane Isaias forced production shut-ins in the Gulf of Mexico. Force majeure incidents and pipeline problems in Kentucky, Texas, West Virginia and elsewhere have curbed supply over the past month. A major Appalachian pipeline outage is also limiting flows.
Producers have also cut voluntarily. With prices near $3 and storage above average, some producers scaled back output in early October. Production held near 108 Bcf/d in the first week of the month as producers responded to weak weather demand.
Regional prices show the effects. Appalachian and Northeast cash prices have fallen sharply relative to Henry Hub as pipeline outages trap supply in the region. Texas Eastern M-2 spot prices have dropped well below Henry Hub from June to October. Meanwhile, maintenance in the Permian Basin is constraining output there.
Production is expected to rebound. The EIA forecasts 2026 production at 112.2 Bcf/d and 2027 production at 116.1 Bcf/d. Gulf of Mexico output is slowly returning after Isaias. Analysts expect production to ramp up ahead of winter to meet higher demand.
The rebound is the main risk to prices. Once hurricane shut-ins reverse and pipeline problems are fixed, production could quickly return to 112 Bcf/d or more. That would add roughly 1 to 4 Bcf/d of supply, enough to push weekly injections back toward 80 to 90 Bcf.
For the forecast, low production is temporary support. Prices could stay firm while output remains near 108 to 111 Bcf/d. A return to 113 Bcf/d would remove that support and push prices back toward $3.00.
LNG Exports: 17.6 Bcf/d in October Despite Plant Maintenance
LNG exports are a key source of demand, and they remain strong despite seasonal maintenance.
Average gas flows to the nine major U.S. LNG export plants were 17.6 Bcf/d so far in October. That is down slightly from 17.9 Bcf/d in September and below the monthly record of 18.8 Bcf/d set in April.
Daily flows have been higher recently. LNG feedgas deliveries reached 18.72 million dekatherms on a recent day, near record levels. Other data show feedgas holding near 18 Bcf/d through October. Feedgas was estimated at 18.9 Bcf/d on October 7.
Maintenance is weighing on flows. Cove Point in Maryland has been offline for maintenance. Golden Pass in Texas has been running about 50% below recent highs. Freeport LNG has been recovering from an outage that took Train 2 offline. Once these plants return to full operation, feedgas could rise above 19 Bcf/d.
New capacity is coming. Sempra Infrastructure is advancing commissioning at Port Arthur LNG in Texas. New startup activity brings the project closer to adding a major new source of demand on the Gulf Coast. Golden Pass is also ramping up.
Global demand supports U.S. LNG. The Middle East conflict has disrupted LNG shipments from Qatar, one of the world’s largest LNG exporters, through the Strait of Hormuz. That has pushed buyers in Europe and Asia toward U.S. cargoes. U.K. and Dutch gas prices have been volatile on Hormuz headlines.
LNG Canada is also growing. The export terminal in Kitimat, British Columbia, rebounded from a July slowdown, lifting feedgas intake and cargo loadings. Canadian gas prices are firming as the winter heating season approaches, supported by rising LNG export activity.
LNG demand is a structural support. U.S. LNG exports have grown steadily, adding several Bcf/d of demand over the past two years. That demand does not depend on U.S. weather, which provides a floor under prices even in mild periods.
For the forecast, LNG exports are a steady positive. A return to 18.5 Bcf/d or more as maintenance ends would add bullish pressure. Any unplanned outage at a major plant would be bearish.
Weather: Mild Through October 29, Then Colder
Weather is the biggest swing factor for natural gas, and the near-term forecast is mild.
Meteorologists expect weather across most of the country to remain milder than normal through October 29 and October 30. That should keep both heating and cooling demand low. The shoulder season between summer and winter is typically the weakest period for gas demand.
